title: Areas from a boundary
objectives: Find an area from a line integral around its boundary.

screens.title: Curl 1 everywhere
screens.prose: By Green, $\oint_C P\,dx + Q\,dy = \iint_D (Q_x - P_y)\,dA$. If the curl is 1 everywhere, the right side is just the area of $D$. The picture shows one candidate field.
screens.question: Which fields have curl 1 everywhere? Select all that apply.

options.why: Its curl is $0 - 1 = -1$: the sign is wrong.
Its curl is $0 - 0 = 0$; it spreads but does not spin.

feedback.correct: $(0, x)$, $(-y, 0)$ and $\left(-\tfrac y2, \tfrac x2\right)$ all have curl 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $Q_x - P_y$ for every option.

explain.text: Each of the three gives $Q_x - P_y = 1$. So for a counterclockwise boundary, $A = \oint_C x\,dy = -\oint_C y\,dx = \tfrac12\oint_C (x\,dy - y\,dx)$.

screens.title: Drag a corner
screens.prose: Three corners are fixed at $(0, 0)$, $(4, 0)$ and $(4, 3)$. The caption computes the area from the boundary alone, as $\tfrac12\oint (x\,dy - y\,dx)$. Drag $D$.
screens.question: Drag $D$ to make the area 12.5.

hints.text: Raising $D$ adds area; moving it right removes some.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Watch the caption as you drag.

explain.text: Every point on the line $4y - 3x = 13$ gives area 12.5, for example $(1, 4)$. The caption never measures the inside: it walks the boundary.

screens.title: An ellipse
screens.prose: The ellipse $x = 3\cos t$, $y = 2\sin t$, $0 \le t \le 2\pi$, runs counterclockwise. Use $A = \tfrac12\oint_C (x\,dy - y\,dx)$.
screens.question: What is the area of the ellipse?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $x\,dy - y\,dx$ first.

byKey.no-half: You dropped the $\tfrac12$: $\oint (x\,dy - y\,dx)$ is twice the area.
byKey.sq: You squared the semi-axes. They enter once each: $3 \times 2$.

explain.text: $x\,dy - y\,dx = 6\cos^2 t\,dt + 6\sin^2 t\,dt = 6\,dt$. Half of $\int_0^{2\pi} 6\,dt$ is $6\pi$.

screens.title: Any ellipse
screens.prose: Repeat with $x = a\cos t$, $y = b\sin t$ for semi-axes $a, b > 0$.
screens.question: What is the area of the ellipse with semi-axes $a$ and $b$?

options.why: The semi-axes enter once each: $x\,dy - y\,dx = ab\,dt$.
That has the units of a length. The area needs $a$ times $b$.
You dropped the $\tfrac12$ in front of the integral.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Redo the last screen with letters.

explain.text: $x\,dy - y\,dx = ab\,dt$, so the area is $\tfrac12 \cdot ab \cdot 2\pi = \pi ab$. A circle is the case $a = b = r$.

screens.title: The shoelace formula
screens.prose: For a polygon with vertices $(x_1, y_1), \dots, (x_n, y_n)$ listed counterclockwise, and $(x_{n+1}, y_{n+1}) = (x_1, y_1)$, we build the area from $A = \tfrac12\oint (x\,dy - y\,dx)$.
screens.question: Put the derivation in order.

lines.text: On the edge from $(x_i, y_i)$ to $(x_{i+1}, y_{i+1})$, take $\mathbf r(t) = (1 - t)(x_i, y_i) + t(x_{i+1}, y_{i+1})$. (Straight edge.)
There $\int (x\,dy - y\,dx) = x_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_i$. (Integrate the linear terms; the $t$ parts cancel.)
Add the edges round the polygon. (The boundary is the chain of edges.)
$A = \tfrac12 \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_i)$. (Area formula with the $\tfrac12$.)
There $\int (x\,dy - y\,dx) = (x_{i+1} - x_i)(y_{i+1} - y_i)$. (Rise times run.)
lines.why: That is the area of a rectangle on the edge, not the line integral along it.

hints.text: On that edge $x\,dy - y\,dx$ integrates to a cross term.
Sum the cross terms and halve.

feedback.correct: The shoelace formula: half the sum of cross terms $x_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_i$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line needs the one before it.

byKey.d1: You used rise times run. The line integral on an edge is the cross term $x_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_i$.
byKey.left-out: All four true lines are needed.

explain.text: On a straight edge $x\,dy - y\,dx$ integrates exactly to the cross term. Summing round a counterclockwise simple polygon and halving gives its area.

screens.title: Shoelace in action
screens.prose: Use the quadrilateral $(0, 0)$, $(4, 0)$, $(4, 3)$, $(1, 4)$, listed counterclockwise, and back to $(0, 0)$.
screens.question: Fill in the cross terms and the area.

feedback.correct: 0, 12, 13 and 0: area 12.5, as you found by dragging.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the order $x_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_i$.

byKey.swap: You took $x_{i+1} y_i - x_i y_{i+1}$. Keep $x_i y_{i+1}$ first: $16 - 3 = 13$.
byKey.no-half: That is the sum. The area is half of it.

explain.text: The cross terms sum to 25, so the area is 12.5. It matches the drag screen with $D = (1, 4)$.

screens.title: An astroid
screens.prose: The astroid $x = \cos^3 t$, $y = \sin^3 t$, $0 \le t \le 2\pi$, has four cusps. There $x\,dy - y\,dx = 3\sin^2 t\cos^2 t\,dt$.
screens.question: What is the area inside the astroid?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Integrate $3\sin^2 t\cos^2 t$, then halve.

byKey.no-half: You left out the $\tfrac12$: $\oint (x\,dy - y\,dx) = \tfrac{3\pi}{4}$ is twice the area.

explain.text: $\tfrac12 \int_0^{2\pi} 3\sin^2 t\cos^2 t\,dt = \tfrac32 \cdot \tfrac{\pi}{4} = \tfrac{3\pi}{8} \approx 1.178$. The cusps cause no trouble: the curve is piecewise smooth.

screens.title: A cardioid, two ways
screens.prose: The cardioid $r = 1 + \cos\theta$ has polar area $\tfrac12\int_0^{2\pi} r^2\,d\theta$. As a curve, $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$ gives $x\,dy - y\,dx = r^2\,d\theta$, so both routes agree.
screens.question: What is the cardioid's area, to 3 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Expand $(1 + \cos\theta)^2$ and integrate each term.

explain.text: $\tfrac12(2\pi + 0 + \pi) = \tfrac{3\pi}{2} \approx 4.712$. The polar formula is Green's area formula in polar form.

screens.title: Order matters
screens.prose: The shoelace formula needs the vertices in order round the boundary. Here are the same four corners, listed as $(0, 0)$, $(4, 3)$, $(4, 0)$, $(1, 4)$.
screens.question: What does the shoelace formula give for this listing?

options.text: 2: the listed path crosses itself, so it is not the quadrilateral's boundary
12.5: the same corners give the same area
options.why: The formula follows the listed path. This order jumps across the shape.

canvas.caption: Listed in this order, the boundary crosses itself.

options.why: Reversing $1, 2, 3, 4$ gives $4, 3, 2, 1$. This listing swaps two corners instead.

canvas.caption: Listed in this order, the boundary crosses itself.

options.why: The bow tie's two loops cancel exactly. Here the two loops are unequal.

canvas.caption: The bow tie: one loop counterclockwise, one clockwise.

hints.text: Draw the path in the listed order.

feedback.correct: 2: the listed path is not the boundary, so the formula measures something else.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute the four cross terms for this order.

byKey.same: You assumed the corners alone fix the area. The formula reads them in the listed order, round a path that crosses itself.

explain.text: The cross terms are $0 - 12 + 16 + 0 = 4$, so the formula gives 2. A crossing path counts its two loops with opposite signs. Clockwise listing of a simple polygon gives minus its area.

canvas.caption: Listed in this order, the boundary crosses itself.

screens.title: Traced twice, and holes
screens.prose: A boundary integral counts each loop of the path. A square ring, the square $[0, 4]^2$ minus $[1, 3]^2$, has an outer and an inner boundary.
screens.question: Which boundary integral gives the ring's area, 12?

options.text: Outer square counterclockwise plus inner square clockwise

options.why: That adds the inner square's area: $16 + 4 = 20$.
That gives 16, the area with the hole filled in.
Tracing twice doubles the area to 32.

hints.text: Green's region must stay on the left of its boundary.
Walking the inner square clockwise keeps the ring on the left.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the ring on your left as you walk each boundary.

explain.text: Counterclockwise outside gives 16; clockwise inside subtracts 4. A path traced twice counts twice, so it would double the area.

screens.title: A market maker's loop
screens.prose: A trader's P&L round a loop in the (inventory, price) plane is $-\oint p\,dq$. Buy 200 at £10.00. Sell 100 while the price rises steadily to £10.30, then 100 while it falls back to £10.00.
screens.question: Fill in each leg's cash and the total.

hints.text: Buying costs cash: the first leg is negative.
Selling 100 as the price moves steadily from £10.00 to £10.30 averages £10.15.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each sale is 100 shares at the average price of its leg.

byKey.sign: Buying pays cash out, so that leg is $-2{,}000$.
byKey.top: The price rises steadily, so the 100 shares average £10.15, not £10.30.

explain.text: The cash totals £30. The triangle $(0, 10)$, $(200, 10)$, $(100, 10.3)$ has shoelace area $\tfrac12 \times 200 \times 0.3 = 30$. A buy at £10.00 and a sell at £10.50 of 100 shares encloses a rectangle of area £50.

screens.title: Which way round
screens.prose: The loop's area is the P&L only with the right sign. In the plane of inventory $q$ across and price $p$ up, the trader buys low then sells high.
screens.question: Which way does a profitable buy-low, sell-high loop run?

options.text: Counterclockwise, so $-\oint p\,dq$ is plus its area

options.why: Buying moves right along the low price; selling moves left along the high price. That is counterclockwise.

options.text: Either way: area is never negative
options.why: A line integral area is signed. Clockwise would give a loss of the same size.

options.text: It does not form a loop
options.why: Inventory and price return to their start, so the path is closed.

hints.text: Buying increases $q$ at the low price.
Selling decreases $q$ at the higher price.
Right along the bottom, left along the top: counterclockwise.

feedback.correct: Counterclockwise: buy low on the bottom edge, sell high on the top.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Trace the trades on the picture.

explain.text: Counterclockwise loops give $-\oint p\,dq = +$area: a profit. Buying high and selling low runs clockwise and loses the area.

ideas: For a region bounded by a piecewise smooth simple closed curve, counterclockwise, $A = \oint x\,dy = -\oint y\,dx = \tfrac12\oint (x\,dy - y\,dx)$.
For a simple polygon listed counterclockwise, $A = \tfrac12\sum (x_i y_{i+1} - x_{i+1} y_i)$, the shoelace formula.
Clockwise gives minus the area, a crossing path mixes signs, and a hole's boundary runs clockwise.

formula.note: C counterclockwise, simple and piecewise smooth.
